This classroom project investigates how different folding techniques affect the load-bearing capacity of simple cardboard bridges. Students constructed three distinct bridge models using identical materials and dimensions, varying only the geometric folds. Each structure was tested by gradually adding weight until failure occurred. Due to the informal setting and limited sample size, this study serves primarily as an educational demonstration rather than rigorous scientific research. Results suggested that triangular folding patterns generally supported more weight than flat designs, though inconsistencies in manual construction likely influenced outcomes. These preliminary observations highlight basic engineering principles but should not be interpreted as definitive data. Further controlled experiments would be necessary to validate these tentative findings accurately.

text: A room can feel stuffy even at a comfortable temperature because temperature is only one part of comfort. High humidity slows the evaporation of moisture from skin, making the air feel heavy and stale. Low airflow matters too: without movement, exhaled carbon dioxide, odors, and heat linger near occupants instead of dispersing. Poor ventilation traps these byproducts, so the space feels close and oppressive. Air conditioning may cool the air but not necessarily reduce humidity or improve circulation. Opening a window, using a fan, or running ventilation can restore a fresher feel by moving air and lowering moisture.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

text: A room may feel stuffy despite a comfortable temperature primarily due to poor ventilation and elevated humidity levels. When airflow is stagnant, carbon dioxide exhaled by occupants accumulates, creating a sense of heaviness or dullness in the air. Simultaneously, high humidity prevents sweat from evaporating efficiently from the skin, which can make the environment feel clammy and oppressive even if the thermometer reads pleasantly. Without adequate circulation from fans, open windows, or HVAC systems, fresh oxygen fails to replace depleted air. This combination of moisture retention and lack of movement disrupts thermal comfort, leading to that characteristic stifling sensation. Improving air exchange effectively mitigates these issues by balancing moisture and replenishing oxygen.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

text: A room can feel stuffy even at a comfortable temperature because comfort depends on more than heat. Humidity matters: when the air holds a lot of moisture, sweat evaporates from your skin more slowly, so the air feels heavy, sticky, and close. Airflow matters too. In still air, a thin layer of warm, moist air tends to cling around your body, and without a breeze to carry it away, the space feels stagnant. Poor ventilation can also let cooking smells, dust, and other odors linger, reinforcing that "used air" impression. Opening a window, running a fan, or using a dehumidifier or exhaust vent often makes the room feel fresher without changing the temperature.

text:
A room can feel incredibly stuffy even at a comfortable temperature due to high humidity and a lack of airflow. 

When relative humidity is high, the air is saturated with moisture. This slows down the rate at which sweat evaporates from your skin, preventing your body's natural cooling process and making the air feel thick and heavy. 

Without active airflow, this stagnant air traps heat, moisture, and carbon dioxide in a localized "envelope" around your body. Without a breeze or ventilation to disperse these elements, the air becomes stale. Essentially, stagnant, moisture-laden air prevents your skin from breathing, turning a thermally comfortable room into a suffocating environment.
